Root Crops
Artichoke, Jerusalem.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn / Winter

Jerusalem artichokes are not true artichokes at all, but vigorous sunflower relatives grown for their knobbly underground tubers. They are hardy, reliable and useful for winter soups, stews and grated salads, with a sweet, nutty flavour which is not to everybody's taste and may not suit every digestion. The plants grow very tall in rich soil, making them useful as a screen or windbreak but also capable of robbing light from lower crops if planted in a long row. They are easy to grow from tubers, but hard to eradicate once established because even small pieces left in the soil can regrow.

Recommended varieties
Fuseau

Smooth, elongated tubers make this a practical kitchen choice, with less fiddly preparation than very knobbly selections.

Dwarf Sunray

A shorter-growing option with pale, relatively smooth tubers. Worth considering where tall Jerusalem artichokes would be awkward.

Small Wonder

A compact Jerusalem artichoke sold for containers and small plots, with tubers clustered near the stem.

Key risks
SCLEROTINIA ROT

Stem bases rot and may carry fluffy white mould with black, seed-like resting bodies.

SLUGS

Slugs may nibble spring shoots; established Jerusalem artichokes usually outgrow light leaf damage.

MICE

Mice may burrow among tubers in winter and eat stored or unlifted roots.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 8

Growing & harvesting
Choose the site carefully.

Tall stems shade neighbours, and missed tubers regrow readily.

Leave tubers until they are needed.

They are hardy in the ground and provide a useful winter crop.

Soil & preparation
Light, sandy or free-draining soil suits the crop, provided it is not very acid or waterlogged in winter. Improve heavy clay before planting.
Prepare in autumn or early winter, removing perennial weeds and adding compost or well-rotted manure where humus is low. Sandy soil needs less preparation, though compost can improve the crop.
Sowing & planting
1 Set the tuber

Plant tubers in late winter or early spring. Choose a clump or block where tall stems will not shade lower crops.

2 Cover carefully

Cover the tubers carefully and water in. Remove stray tuber fragments when clearing the bed; they can regrow.

Tuber depth 6 in.
Rows 3 ft between rows
Plants / blocks 12 in. between plants
Looking after the crop
Hoe between young plants or mulch deeply against weeds, especially on heavy ground. Established plants on light soil need little attention.
Earth up the bases when stems are about 1 ft tall. Water during dry weather, especially on light soil.
In windy sites, support both sides of the row with wires between sturdy end canes. Tall stems can also make a temporary windbreak.
Leave flowers for pollinators if desired. Give weak plants an appropriate organic liquid feed during summer.
Harvesting & storage
After leaves yellow in autumn, cut stems about 3 in. above soil. Use healthy tops as mulch or weave them into a temporary windbreak.
Lift tubers as needed from late autumn through early spring. They are hardy, but frozen ground can prevent access: lift a supply before a hard freeze.
Reserve sound tubers for replanting. Remove unwanted tubers and fragments carefully because even small pieces can regrow.
When clearing a bed, revisit it through spring and repeatedly remove shoots and their tubers. One lifting may not clear the crop completely.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
SCLEROTINIA ROT	White mould and black bodies in rotting stems.	Remove infected plants and debris; avoid spreading affected soil.
SLUGS	Spring leaves nibbled; tubers hollowed.	Inspect and hand-pick; lift mature tubers before damage worsens.
MICE	Tubers are gnawed; tunnels may be present.	Rodent-proof stored tubers and inspect regularly.
Final tips

Keep the tall plants north of shorter vegetables so the screen does not rob them of light.

A manageable clump is often easier to accommodate than a long shading row.

In severe frost, cover stem bases with straw or lift tubers after the tops have died back.

Protect stored tubers from rodents and inspect them regularly for damage or decay.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 9

Root Crops
Beetroot.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Beetroot’s sweet, earthy roots suit raw salads, hot dishes, pickles, borsch and chutneys; young leaves are edible too. This cool-climate crop needs well-drained, humus-rich soil and steady moisture. Growth starts slowly, then roots swell quickly. Sow small batches or raise module clumps. Early sowings under cover can give golf-ball-sized roots by late spring; later sowings provide summer, autumn and storage crops. Lift before roots become woody or leathery. In mild winters some can stay outside, but severe frost can freeze and rot them.

Recommended varieties
GLOBE · RED
Boltardy

A familiar round red beetroot valued for resistance to bolting. A useful choice for earlier sowings under suitable conditions.

GLOBE · RED
Pablo F1

A round red beetroot producing uniform roots with good kitchen quality. Harvest young for tender roots.

CYLINDRICAL
Cylindra

Long, cylindrical red roots make even slices easy. Useful for cooking and pickling when shape matters more than round presentation.

GLOBE · RED
Chioggia

A heritage beetroot with pink-and-white rings when cut raw. Grow for visual variety alongside a standard red beetroot.

CYLINDRICAL
Forono

An elongated red beetroot with a tidy shape for slicing. Retain as an established alternative to round-rooted selections.

Key risks
Bolting

Plants sometimes run to seed before roots have developed.

Fanging

Forked roots are usually caused by adding fresh manure shortly before sowing.

Mangold Fly (Leaf Miner)

Small white grubs burrow inside the leaves, causing tunnels which later turn into blisters.

Heart Rot

Leaves wilt in summer and the tops of the roots develop brown, sunken patches.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 10

Growing & harvesting
A cool-climate crop.

Use well-drained soil rich in organic matter.

Keep moisture steady.

Drought hardens roots; sudden wet can split them.

Sow for a long season.

Successive sowings extend the harvest.

Soil & preparation
Use humus-rich, well-drained soil without fresh manure. Remove stones; long roots need deep, sandy ground.
Use previously manured ground or add autumn compost. Lime acid soil towards pH 6.5; feed poor ground if needed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow seed clusters

Sow clusters thinly; cover and keep moist.

2 Thin seedlings

Thin direct sowings early to single plants.

Raise early crops in modules; plant clumps intact. Quick facts spacing is for individual, direct-sown plants.

Soak clusters for hours or overnight. Sow warm for early-spring planting; continue into early summer for roots before winter.

Looking after the crop
Thin direct sowings early to single plants; protect from birds. Plant module clumps intact and pick their largest roots first.
Hoe gently; water evenly and moderately. Mulch to hold moisture: drought makes roots woody and reduces yield; sudden wet can split them.
Fleece can bring crops forward, but weed beneath it regularly. Pick young leaves before they toughen and use them like spinach.
Harvesting & storage
Pull globe roots before cricket-ball size. Gently twist larger roots from clumps, letting smaller ones swell; well-kept patches can crop for two months or more.
Fork up storage roots in autumn without piercing them. Discard damaged roots. Twist off foliage, leaving short stalks; do not cut roots.
Roots can stay outside in mild winters, but lift before severe frost. Store sound roots cool in paper sacks or moist sand, without touching.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	Early flowering; poor roots.	Avoid early sowing; thin promptly; use resistant varieties.
Fanging	Forked roots.	Avoid fresh manure and stones; prepare soil well.
Mangold Fly (Leaf Miner)	Blisters and tunnels in leaves.	Crush larvae in mines; use mesh on a rotated bed.
Heart Rot	Brown or black areas inside roots.	Confirm boron shortage; seek organic correction advice.
Blackleg	Seedlings blacken and collapse.	Remove affected seedlings; improve drainage.
Speckled Yellows	Yellow patches; rolled edges.	Confirm manganese shortage; avoid excess lime.
Autumnal Fungal Root Rots	Dark rot in wet autumns.	Lift promptly; store only sound roots.
Leaf Spot	Brown spots with pale centres.	Remove badly affected leaves; rotate; add compost.
Final tips

Leave four or five seedlings in module clumps.

Take the largest clump roots first, leaving others to swell.

Twist off foliage; do not cut roots for storage.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 11

Root Crops
Carrot.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Steady moisture, careful thinning and carrot-fly protection make a big difference. Fresh manure, compaction, stones, drought and rough handling can leave roots forked, tough or damaged.

Recommended varieties
SHORT-ROOTED
Early Nantes 2

A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Autumn King

A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Chantenay Red Cored

A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

Key risks
Carrot Fly

Tell-tale signs on carrots are reddish leaves which wilt in sunny weather and later turn yellow.

Fanging

Fanging is usually caused by adding manure or compost to the soil shortly before seed sowing.

Small Roots

Aphids and virus will stunt growth and reduce yield, but even in the absence of pests and diseases many gardeners produce disappointingly small carrots.

Splitting

Much more serious than fanging of carrots, because the roots will not store.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 12

Growing & harvesting
Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow thinly

Sow direct, very thinly, in shallow drills.

2 Cover lightly

Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.

3 Thin later

Thin seedlings to the final spacing in Quick facts.

Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist.

Looking after the crop
Thin only where needed, in the evening or damp weather; water dry soil first. Firm afterwards and remove thinnings: bruised roots attract carrot fly.
Weed small seedlings carefully. Avoid hoeing close to established carrots or loosening soil around roots.
Water deeply and evenly in dry spells, soaking to root depth. Light surface watering is ineffective; sudden heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare to reduce slug shelter; clear early weeds before later sowings.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take only eight weeks. Work from one row end, easing roots with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, sooner if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Late-autumn growth is slow; standing roots face more slug and maggot damage and may split.
Store sound roots with leaves trimmed about 1/2 in. above the crown. Keep separate in sand, cool and ventilated just above freezing. Check for rot; sound roots can keep until March.
GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 13

Carrot · continued
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Carrot Fly	Tunnelled roots.	Use fine mesh; remove thinnings; avoid bruising.
Fanging	Forked roots	Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.
Small Roots	Small roots; weak growth.	Improve soil; use organic feed if growth is poor.
Splitting	Split roots.	Water evenly; mulch in drought; use split roots now.
Sclerotinia Rot	White mould; rotting roots.	Remove diseased roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Carrot-Willow Aphid	Distorted, stunted leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Black Rot	Black lesions on stored roots.	Remove rotten roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Motley Dwarf Virus	Yellow mottling; red outer leaves.	No cure; remove affected plants. Monitor aphids.
Green Top	Green exposed crowns.	Earth up to cover exposed root tops.
Violet Root Rot	Purple felt-like growth on roots.	Destroy affected roots; never store them; rotate.
Final tips

Avoid fresh manure and disturbance around established roots.

Work from one end of the row when harvesting.

Inspect stored roots and remove any that rot.

IMPERIAL · 14

Root Crops
Celeriac.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Autumn

Celeriac, or turnip-rooted celery, is grown for its swollen stem-base. Its earthy celery flavour suits soups, stews, salads and winter dishes; lifted roots keep into spring if stored cool. It needs less blanching and earthing-up work than celery, but still needs a full season, a good start under cover and rich, moisture-retentive soil. Shallow, fibrous roots suffer in dry ground: water steadily in dry weather. Heavy, well-composted soil suits it well; varieties are broadly similar.

Mar – Apr

Harvest

Oct – Nov

Row spacing

Recommended varieties
Prinz

A dependable celeriac for rounded roots and useful kitchen quality. A strong first choice for the main crop.

Monarch

A modern celeriac with pale flesh and comparatively smooth roots. A useful addition for easier preparation in the kitchen.

Asterix F1

An early hybrid producing large, round roots for autumn harvesting and storage. Useful bolting resistance helps support a dependable crop.

Giant Prague

A long-established celeriac with large roots. Retain as a heritage alternative where seed cost and traditional varieties matter.

Key risks
SLUGS

Slugs can damage seedlings and later chew holes in swollen roots.

CARROT FLY

Brown lines or tunnels across the lower part of the root may be caused by carrot root fly maggots.

FROST

Celeriac is hardy, but exposed roots and frozen ground can make winter harvesting difficult.

Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)

Celery leaf miner makes pale blotches that turn brown and papery.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 16

Growing & harvesting
Keep growth steady from the start.

Cold or drought checks can reduce the crop and encourage bolting.

Keep the crown at soil level.

Celeriac needs no celery-style earthing up or blanching.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of well-rotted compost. Improved heavier ground often suits shallow-rooted celeriac.
Mulch to conserve moisture; add an appropriate organic feed only if the soil lacks fertility.
Sowing & planting
1 Surface sow

Sow March–April under cover. Moist compost; barely cover seed.

2 Grow on

Prick out into modules. Avoid cold and drought; harden off before planting.

3 Keep the crown clear

Plant after late frosts, stem-base at soil level. Firm and water; do not earth up.

Looking after the crop
Weed until leaves cover the ground. Water in dry weather and maintain a compost mulch: shallow roots dry quickly, checking the swollen stem-base’s growth.
Keep soil and mulch off crowns; draw back soil displaced by hoeing. Remove side shoots, damaged leaves and mature horizontal outer leaves. Keep healthy upright foliage; never earth up like celery.
Harvesting & storage
Harvest autumn–winter. Sound roots can stay in well-drained soil, under straw in cold spells. On wet sites, lift for storage, often in October–November before winter waterlogging.
Loosen with a spade or trowel, severing fleshy roots as you lift. Trim storage roots lightly; pack cool in moist coir or peat-free compost against drying. Check for decay.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
SLUGS	Seedlings chewed; holes in mature roots.	Check and hand-pick; lift damaged roots before rot develops.
CARROT FLY	Brown tunnels across the swollen base.	Use insect mesh; avoid damage during weeding.
FROST	Exposed swollen bases are frost-damaged.	Use straw in cold spells; lift and store on wet or exposed sites.
Celery Fly (Leaf Miner)	Pale blotch mines in leaves.	Tolerate light damage; remove badly mined leaf parts.
Bolting	Flower stems replace useful root growth.	Avoid cold and drought checks; harden off gradually.
Celery Leaf Spot (Blight)	Brown spots spread through leaves.	Use healthy seed; remove affected leaves and avoid splashing.
HOLLOW OR HOLED ROOTS	Internal hollows or pest holes.	Keep moisture even; inspect and discard rotten tissue.
Damping Off	Seedlings rot at the base and collapse.	Use clean compost; avoid overwatering and improve airflow.
WOODLICE	Woodlice occupy existing root holes.	Check for earlier slug damage or rot; harvest sound parts promptly.
Final tips

Fleece can help newly planted seedlings establish; keep them growing without cold or dry checks.

Check stored roots regularly and remove any that begin to rot.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 17

Root Crops
Kohl Rabi.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Kohl rabi looks like a root crop, but the edible globe is really a swelling of the stem just above ground level. It is a cabbage relative with a sweet, mild brassica flavour and a delicate texture when grown quickly and picked young. The crop matures fast, often in about 8-12 weeks, making it useful as a half-season brassica. Quality depends on steady moisture and timely harvesting: drought, checks to growth or leaving the globes too long can make them hard and woody. Small young globes are good raw or cooked, while larger late varieties can stand into autumn if they keep growing steadily.

Recommended varieties
Kolibri F1

A quick-growing purple kohlrabi with crisp white flesh. Pick the swollen stems young for tender raw or cooked slices.

Kossak F1

A pale-green kohlrabi with mild white flesh. A useful modern alternative to the traditional Vienna selections.

White Superschmelz

A large-growing pale kohlrabi. Useful for gardeners wanting a substantial crop rather than very small, quick-picked stems.

Key risks
Woody Kohl Rabi

Drought, growth checks, crowding or delayed harvesting make the swollen stem hard and fibrous.

Flea Beetle

Tiny jumping beetles chew small round holes in young leaves, especially in warm dry weather.

Cabbage Caterpillars

Caterpillars of cabbage white butterfly, cabbage moth and related pests chew holes in leaves.

Club Root (Finger and Toe)

Swollen, distorted roots cause poor growth and wilting in sunshine.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 18

Growing & harvesting
Keep moisture steady.

Dry soil and growth checks make the stem woody.

Harvest while tender.

Do not wait for ordinary varieties to become oversized.

Hoe shallowly.

Avoid disturbing the roots while plants are small.

Soil & preparation
Choose a sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. Test soil before adding lime.
Steady moisture matters: dry soil and growth checks make the swollen stem hard and woody.
Prepare the bed early with mature compost where needed. Give roots room and steady moisture; the edible globe is a swollen stem above ground.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow shallowly

Sow thinly where plants will crop. Cover lightly; start in April and sow in succession through early summer, then again in July for a late crop.

2 Thin young plants

Start at the first true leaves and thin gradually to final spacing. Keep plants growing steadily; water in dry weather to avoid woody stems.

Plant hardened modules before they exceed 2 in. tall, at 6 in. in rows 12 in. apart. Allow more room for giant varieties.

Looking after the crop
Thin promptly. Protect young plants from birds; use collars or mesh where root fly is a problem.
Weed carefully. Check moisture and pests if growth slows; use an organic feed where fertility is poor.
Water in dry spells to prevent tough, woody globes. Give larger autumn crops extra room as growth slows in falling temperatures.
Harvesting & storage
Pull globes young and tender, from golf-ball to roughly tennis-ball size. Only grow suitable varieties larger; others become woody.
Late crops can stand through autumn and, in mild areas, into December. Protect with fleece or cloches before wintry weather and harvest while still tender.
Fresh-pulled globes are best. Keep briefly in cool conditions; quality declines after lifting.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Woody Kohl Rabi	Hard, fibrous globes.	Water steadily; space well and harvest young.
Flea Beetle	Tiny holes; jumping beetles.	Mesh young plants; keep growth steady.
Cabbage Caterpillars	Holes; feeding caterpillars.	Hand-pick eggs and larvae; use fine mesh.
Club Root (Finger and Toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage Root Fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Use collars or mesh on a rotated bed.
Slugs and Snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; clear yellow leaves near seedlings.
Pigeons	Pecked or stripped leaves.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Mealy Aphid	Grey colonies; curled leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Final tips

Sow two or three small batches from April to June.

Try White Superschmelz for a July sowing and late crop.

Moist soil and timely picking keep globes tender.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 19

Root Crops
Parsnip.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Parsnips are slow, deep-rooting biennials grown for white tap roots that sweeten as cold turns starch to sugar. They occupy the ground for a long season and seedlings emerge slowly, but established plants need little beyond weed control and moisture while young. Use fresh seed: cold or dry soil and sowing too deeply can leave a blank row. Deep, humus-rich, stone-free ground gives the best roots, preferably undug or improved for an earlier crop; avoid fresh manure.

Recommended varieties
Gladiator

A well-established hybrid parsnip producing useful, even roots. A strong first choice for the main autumn and winter crop.

Tender and True

A traditional parsnip grown for long roots and good flavour. Keep as the familiar open-pollinated alternative.

Palace F1

An early-to-maincrop hybrid with smooth roots, shallow crowns and some canker resistance. A useful alternative to Gladiator.

Key risks
CANKER

In wet winters, heavy soils, acid soil or ground containing fresh manure, the tops of roots may develop brown or black fungal rot.

POOR GERMINATION

Parsnip seed loses viability quickly.

CARROT ROOT FLY

Carrot fly larvae tunnel into parsnip roots, leaving rusty-brown scars and making damaged roots vulnerable to rot.

FORKING

Forked roots are usually caused by stones, heavy soil, fresh manure, lumpy compost or ground that has not been improved deeply enough in advance.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 20

Growing & harvesting
Use fresh seed and sow in place.

Germination is slow; keep the seedbed moist while you wait.

Prepare for long, straight roots.

Avoid stones, compaction and fresh manure just before sowing.

Soil & preparation
Choose deep, friable, stone-free soil improved for a previous crop. Shorter varieties suit shallower or heavier ground.
Avoid fresh manure/lumpy compost. Rake clean; test acid soil before liming to pH 6.5.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow fresh seed

Sow fresh seed thinly, or 3 per station. Cover with fine soil/compost; firm.

2 Thin in place

Keep strongest seedlings; discard thinnings. Do not transplant.

Keep drills moist while seeds germinate. A few radish seeds can mark the row.

March–April is more reliable than cold February soil. Weed first for May–early June sowings, which give smaller roots and may reduce canker.

Looking after the crop
Thin carefully, weed while seedlings are small and avoid disturbing crowns or roots.
Keep young plants moist: early checks reduce yield, although mature roots reach deep moisture. Mulch between rows with fine mature compost, especially on low-humus soil; keep crowns clear and stop weeds seeding.
Harvesting & storage
Lift useful roots from autumn; cold improves sweetness and dry weather can make lifting cleaner. Loosen deeply with a fork and ease out: pulling against firm ground snaps long tap roots.
Leave roots in the ground through winter where lifting remains practical. Lift a batch before hard freezes and store in damp sand, cool and frost-free.
Finish the crop before spring regrowth and flowering make roots woody.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
CANKER	Brown or black rot at root crowns.	Resistant varieties; avoid damage and fresh manure.
POOR GERMINATION	Seedlings fail to appear.	Use fresh seed; keep moist and resow while season allows.
CARROT ROOT FLY	Rusty-brown scars and tunnels in roots; damaged roots may rot.	Cover with insect-proof mesh from sowing; secure every edge.
FORKING	Roots divide into several forks.	Remove stones; avoid compaction and fresh manure.
LEAF MINER	Blistered leaf mines with maggots.	Tolerate light damage; remove badly mined leaf parts.
Sclerotinia Rot	White woolly mould and soft rot.	Discard affected roots; keep stores clean and airy.
Violet Root Rot	Purplish felt-like threads coat roots.	Discard affected roots; avoid storing suspect roots.
Final tips

A few radishes mark slow-germinating rows and can be harvested before parsnips need the space.

Lift only what you need while winter soil remains workable; keep stored roots from drying out.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 21

Root Crops
Potato.
DIFFICULTY

Recommended varieties
Zefa Fino

An established Florence fennel grown for swollen leaf bases. Keep growth steady with moisture and use appropriate sowing dates.

Romanesco

A traditional Florence fennel with substantial bulbs. Retain for gardeners who prefer a familiar non-hybrid selection.

Rondo F1

A modern Florence fennel producing rounded bulbs. A useful addition to the established open-pollinated choices.

Key risks
BOLTING OR STEMMY BULBS

Cold while young, drought and root disturbance can trigger premature flowering.

SMALL OR DRY BULBS

Drought and poor fertility produce small, less juicy bulbs.

LOWER SHEATH ROT

Lower sheaths may soften and decay.

FROST

Hard frost damages bulbs.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 98

Growing & harvesting
Keep growth steady and moist.

Drought, crowding and root disturbance can spoil bulb development.

Match sowing time to the variety.

Summer sowings usually give more reliable UK autumn bulbs.

Soil & preparation
Deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of humus gives tender, juicy bulbs.
Prepare with well-rotted manure or compost before sowing or planting. Avoid waterlogging.
A compost dressing about 2 in. deep, spread well before planting, feeds the crop and helps hold summer moisture.
Sowing & planting
1 Raise in modules

Sow in modules under cover from May, or outdoors in June–July. Keep young plants warm and growing steadily.

2 Plant level

Plant actively growing seedlings with rootballs intact, at module depth. Keep the growing point above soil; water well.

Direct-sown plants Between plants: 12 in. for full bulbs; 6 in. for baby bulbs

June and July sowings are useful after spring cabbage, spinach or salads. Earlier sowing needs a suitable variety and protected conditions; avoid leaving module plants to become checked.

Looking after the crop
Keep moisture even as bulbs swell: drought reduces juiciness and encourages bolting. Dress light or depleted soil with compost.
Hoe or hand-weed while plants are young: small plants compete poorly with weeds.
Thin direct-sown rows promptly. Crowded plants make smaller, less well-shaped bulbs and may run up to stem.
Earth up lightly where useful to keep the base tender and moist, without covering the growing centre or trapping rot around old sheaths.
Harvesting & storage
Cut tender bulbs before they turn fibrous or frost arrives: baby bulbs about 2 in. across, full bulbs about 4–6 in. Harvest elongating small bulbs promptly; they are unlikely to fatten.
Trim tough stems and use fronds for flavouring. Lift before hard frost; keep sound autumn bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.
If lower sheaths rot, lift promptly, discard rotten tissue and use only firm sound parts; discard extensively rotted bulbs.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
BOLTING OR STEMMY BULBS	Small bulbs elongate or start flowering.	Harvest usable parts; match sowing dates to variety.
SMALL OR DRY BULBS	Bulbs stay small and lose juiciness.	Use compost, mulch and steady watering.
LOWER SHEATH ROT	Outer sheaths soften and decay.	Lift promptly; discard rot and use only sound tissue.
FROST	Bulbs deteriorate after freezing.	Harvest before hard frost; store sound bulbs frost-free.
Final tips

Raise modules as an early crop finishes; plant before roots become pot-bound.

Harvest stemmy bulbs promptly; they are unlikely to fatten later.

Compost mulch on light or depleted soil conserves summer moisture.

Pick for tenderness before frost, fibrous growth or decay; size alone is no guide.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 99

Rhubarb.

Spring / Summer

Rhubarb is a long-lived perennial vegetable, usually cooked as fruit. Large crowns give tart spring stems, green to red by variety; green stems are edible and colour does not show ripeness. Never eat the leaves. It suits cool climates and winter dormancy. Moist, drained, compost-rich soil, feeding, mulching, spring watering and flower removal keep crowns cropping for years. Yield varies with variety, age and conditions; leave enough foliage to rebuild the crown.

Recommended varieties
Timperley Early

Early pink-and-green stems; also good for forcing to start the season.

Victoria

Established main-season crop of substantial green-red stalks for pies and preserves.

Raspberry Red

Tender, flavoursome red stalks. Buy named crowns/plants for consistency.

Glaskin's Perpetual

Traditional, economical seed-raised rhubarb; expect variation between plants.

Key risks
CROWN ROT

Decay at the crown can cause weak, dull stems and rotting buds.

SLUGS UNDER FORCING POTS

Slugs may hide inside forcing pots or buckets and damage the tender forced stems.

POOR GROWTH OR STRINGY STEMS

Usually linked to dry soil, lack of organic matter, overcropping, or forcing the same crown too often.

HONEY FUNGUS

Honey fungus can cause rhubarb crowns to decline and die.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 100

Growing & harvesting
Let young crowns build strength.

Leave the first year unpicked and take only a light crop in the second.

Eat the stalks, never the leaves.

Twist stalks away cleanly and leave plenty of foliage to feed the crown.

Soil & preparation
Choose a permanent, open position with rich, moist but well-drained soil. Avoid winter waterlogging and clear perennial weeds.
Prepare with compost, leaf mould or rotted manure. Rhubarb tolerates slightly acid soil; do not lime routinely. Allow space for vigorous roots at a plot edge.
Sowing & planting
1 Set the crown

Buy a crown or divide a vigorous piece in winter dormancy. Set upright, buds/new shoots just above soil.

2 Firm and water

Firm and water. Keep new shoots clear; allow room for a large permanent clump.

Seed is an alternative: grow young plants on for late-summer or autumn planting. Crowns preserve named varieties and crop sooner.

Looking after the crop
Mulch annually with compost or well-rotted manure, keeping the central crown clear.
Water during dry spells, especially in spring: dry soil gives shorter, thinner and more stringy stalks.
Remove flower stalks promptly so energy goes into useful leaves and stems.
Force a strong, established crown in late winter under a light-proof pot. Check slugs. Remove cover after picking; rest for the season and never force in consecutive years.
Harvesting & storage
Leave new crowns unpicked in year one; take a light second-year crop. At each picking leave at least two-thirds of the stems and all thin ones.
Mature plants crop in spring and early summer; stop the usual harvest by late June so leaves rebuild the crown.
Grip near the base, twist and pull gently; avoid cut stumps. Remove and compost the poisonous leaf; eat only the stalk.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
CROWN ROT	Bud and crown decay; stems become weak.	Remove badly affected crowns; improve drainage and use a clean site.
SLUGS UNDER FORCING POTS	Tender forced stems are chewed.	Check beneath forcing covers weekly and hand-remove slugs.
POOR GROWTH OR STRINGY STEMS	Thin, weak growth or stringy stems.	Water, mulch and reduce picking; rest over-forced crowns.
HONEY FUNGUS	Declining crown; white fungal sheets in infected roots or crown.	Confirm diagnosis; remove infected roots and woody material.
FLOWERING	Flower stalks rise above the leaves.	Remove flower stalks promptly to conserve the crown.
Final tips

After forcing, take no more stalks that season and do not force the same crown the following year.

Healthy crown divisions retain a named variety; seedlings take longer and may vary.

Divide an ageing or crowded crown during dormancy and retain vigorous healthy pieces.

Leaves are not edible. Compost them and use only the stalks in the kitchen.

This guide covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown in prepared mushroom compost away from direct sun. Fresh ready-spawned kits in bags, buckets or boxes are the simplest route to small crops while outdoor beds are quiet. Check the start-by date and begin promptly: pre-started kits may already be largely colonised. Follow the supplier’s stages, casing and temperatures. Preparing compost from raw ingredients needs controlled composting and conditioning; other mushroom species need different substrates and conditions.

Key risks
PESTS

Mushroom flies can infest compost and damage developing mushrooms.

Contaminating moulds

Contaminating fungi can discolour mushroom substrate or distort and decay developing mushrooms.

Poor cropping

Slow colonisation or stalled cropping may result from unsuitable temperatures, moisture or ventilation.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 102

Growing & harvesting
Start with prepared mushroom compost.

A fresh ready-spawned kit is the simplest route for small quantities.

Keep conditions steady.

Avoid direct sun, temperature extremes and waterlogged casing.

Soil & preparation
Button mushrooms need prepared mushroom compost, not garden soil. Buy fresh spawned compost or a kit. Commercial compost often uses straw, manure and gypsum, processed before spawning.
Home preparation needs initial composting plus controlled pasteurisation and conditioning to remove ammonia. Looks or a fixed number of turns cannot prove readiness; use a complete tested method and suitable equipment.
After colonisation, button mushrooms need a moist casing layer. Follow the kit’s casing material and timing; keep moist, never saturated. Other species may not need casing.
Establishing the crop
1 Start with spawned compost

Buy fresh ready-spawned compost in a bag, bucket or box. Shade from direct sun.

2 Maintain moisture

For supplied compost, add casing as instructed; water lightly to keep moist, never saturated.

Looking after the crop
Spawn growth and cropping need different temperatures: follow each kit stage. Keep conditions steady and ventilated, with no direct sun.
Colonising compost generates heat. Avoid overheating; follow the supplier’s range, as no single maximum suits all strains/kits.
Many button kits crop at 61–64°F; follow the supplier’s range. Water casing carefully to keep lightly moist, never saturated.
Harvesting & storage
Pick before the veil opens for closed buttons, later for open caps. Flushes alternate with rests; timing and duration depend on kit and conditions.
Twist buttons gently to lift without much disturbance. Trim dirty bases and remove broken remnants; refill holes with suitable casing if the kit advises.
After the last crop, compost healthy spent substrate or use as soil improver. Weather first near seedlings/salt-sensitive plants: mushroom compost can contain high soluble salts. Start with fresh prepared material.
Between flushes, use clean water to maintain the kit’s recommended moisture and wait. Once exhausted, remove substrate, then wash, rinse and dry reusable containers.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
PESTS	Small flies appear; larvae damage mushrooms or compost.	Use clean equipment, exclude flies and remove spent or infested material.
Contaminating moulds	Unusual coloured mould or misshapen, decaying mushrooms.	Isolate affected kits; ask the supplier and discard contaminated material.
Poor cropping	Spawn runs poorly or cropping stalls.	Check kit temperature, moisture and airflow; avoid sun and saturation.
Final tips

Use fresh kits and check the supplier’s start-by date rather than storing them indefinitely.

Grow from identified cultivated spawn; do not treat an unknown mushroom appearing nearby as part of the crop.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 103

Bean and Pea
Troubles

Start with the affected part: missing seedlings, marked leaves or damaged pods. Broad beans are prone to blackfly and chocolate spot; peas to weevils, moth caterpillars and mildew. Tender beans need warm soil and steady moisture, particularly at flowering. Not every leaf mark needs treatment.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

PEA / BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Seed Beetle

Tunnelled seeds

RECOGNISE

Small round holes in stored pea or bean seeds contain seed-beetle grubs. Damaged seed may fail or give weak plants.

ACT

Do not sow visibly holed seed; there is no useful repair.

PREVENT

Buy good-quality seed and inspect it before sowing.

PEA

Leaf and Pod Spot

Dry spots on pods

RECOGNISE

Sunken brown spots mark pea pods; peas may discolour. Similar stem and leaf spots can merge in severe wet-weather attacks.

ACT

Remove and destroy badly diseased plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and clear affected crop remains.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Mice
RECOGNISE

Seeds or seedlings disappear, often overnight or under cover. Birds and larger animals can leave similar losses.

ACT

Check the pattern of damage before deciding which animal to exclude.

PREVENT

Raise vulnerable seed in pots or modules. Protect outdoor sowings with suitable physical barriers.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

No Flowers
RECOGNISE

Immaturity, shade, drought or excessive nitrogen can delay flowers. Inspect buds for feeding damage.

ACT

Check buds for damage and review feeding rather than adding more nitrogen.

PREVENT

Use balanced nutrition appropriate to the soil, not heavy nitrogen feeding.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Bean Seed Fly

Tunnelled seedlings

RECOGNISE

Grubs tunnel into bean seeds and seedlings. Seeds fail; emerged plants wilt or distort. Early sowings are most vulnerable.

ACT

Remove damaged seedlings.

PREVENT

Prepare a good seedbed, or start plants in compost-filled pots before planting out.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Birds

Torn pods

RECOGNISE

Pigeons eat seeds and young leaves; sparrows tear pea pods. Birds may pull young beans or damage runner-bean flowers.

ACT

Protect the crop as soon as damage appears.

PREVENT

Use securely supported netting or wire guards; keep it taut, clear of plants and check for trapped wildlife.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 104

Bean and Pea
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Black Bean Aphid

Aphids on leaves

RECOGNISE

Dense black colonies on soft broad-bean tips can stunt growth and distort flowers and pods. French beans may be affected in midsummer.

ACT

Pinch off infested broad-bean tips; squash small colonies where needed. Allow natural predators time to act.

PREVENT

Pinch broad-bean tops at full flower or after the first pods form. Avoid late sowing where attacks recur.

PEA

Pea Aphid

Aphids on leaves

RECOGNISE

Large aphid colonies can check pea growth and damage flowers, although small numbers rarely cause serious trouble.

ACT

Monitor first; squash damaging colonies by hand and let natural predators help.

PREVENT

Encourage aphid predators and keep checking tender growth. Complete exclusion is rarely practical.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Pea and Bean Weevil

Notched leaves

RECOGNISE

U-shaped notches appear along young leaf edges. Grey-brown adults drop when disturbed. Established plants usually outgrow the damage.

ACT

Water seedlings in dry weather to support recovery. Severe damage matters most on small plants.

PREVENT

Raise strong plants and protect vulnerable young crops with insect-proof mesh where attacks recur.

PEA

Pea Thrips

Silvery pods

RECOGNISE

Tiny dark or yellowish insects cause silver patches and small holes on leaves and pods. Hot, dry weather favours damaging attacks.

ACT

Check for insects; water stressed plants, encourage predators and tolerate minor damage.

PREVENT

Keep plants watered and growing steadily; clear the crop after harvest.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 105

Bean and Pea
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

No Pods
RECOGNISE

Runner-bean flowers fall without pods after drought or hot weather; cool weather may reduce pollination. French beans can also drop flowers when dry.

ACT

Water roots thoroughly during dry spells, especially from flowering. Check for flower damage by birds.

PREVENT

Maintain root moisture, mulch and water during flowering. Plant after frost risk and protect flowers from damage.

PEA

Pea Moth

Maggoty peas

RECOGNISE

Pale caterpillars feed inside pods, leaving damaged peas and frass. Flowering crops are vulnerable during summer egg laying.

ACT

Once caterpillars enter pods there is no useful treatment. Discard affected peas when shelling.

PREVENT

Use early or late sowings to avoid peak moth activity, or cover with insect-proof mesh before flowering.

PEA

Marsh Spot

Brown-centred peas

RECOGNISE

A brown-lined cavity inside peas, sometimes with slight yellowing between leaf veins, indicates possible manganese shortage.

ACT

Existing damaged peas cannot be repaired. Confirm the deficiency before adding trace elements.

PREVENT

Improve soil with compost and check pH. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if the shortage is confirmed.

BEAN, BROAD

Chocolate Spot

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Chocolate-brown spots on broad-bean leaves can merge; stems, flowers and pods may also be affected. Cool, damp, crowded crops are most at risk.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants and clear infected remains after cropping.

PREVENT

Improve spacing and airflow. Do not save infected seed; consider spring sowing if autumn crops repeatedly suffer.

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Halo Blight

Spots on leaves

RECOGNISE

Water-soaked leaf spots with yellow halos and wet-looking pod lesions may indicate bacterial halo blight.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased plants.

PREVENT

Use healthy bought seed. Remove diseased debris, rotate crops and avoid handling wet foliage.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 106

Bean and Pea
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER

Anthracnose

Dry spots on pods

RECOGNISE

Sunken dark pod spots, stem cankers and brown leaf patches may develop pinkish margins on French and runner beans.

ACT

Remove badly diseased plants. Confirm the diagnosis before taking further action.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, space for airflow and never save seed from affected plants.

PEA

Downy Mildew

Mouldy leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow patches above pea leaves correspond to mauve or brown mould below. Cool, wet weather favours infection; pods may distort.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and severely diseased plants.

PREVENT

Rotate crops, reduce crowding and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. Water early if foliage will get wet.

PEA

Powdery Mildew
RECOGNISE

White powdery patches affect leaves and sometimes pods, often on late crops. Dry roots and crowded growth increase stress.

ACT

Remove badly affected growth where practical; clear exhausted late crops.

PREVENT

Maintain root moisture and airflow. Choose resistant varieties for late crops where mildew recurs.

BEAN, FRENCH / PEA

Grey Mould (Botrytis)

Rotten pods

RECOGNISE

Softly rotting pods or stems develop fuzzy grey mould, especially in wet weather and crowded crops.

ACT

Remove mouldy pods and damaged material promptly.

PREVENT

Keep picking, avoid crowding and improve airflow; minimise prolonged wet foliage.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Fusarium Wilt

Brown-streaked tissue

RECOGNISE

Stunting, yellow or rolled leaves and poor cropping may accompany reddish-brown streaks inside a cut stem, without outside browning.

ACT

Remove affected plants. Confirm the cause: wilting alone is not a diagnosis.

PREVENT

Choose wilt-resistant varieties where this disease has been confirmed.

BEAN, BROAD / BEAN, FRENCH / BEAN, RUNNER / PEA

Foot Rot and Root Rot

Blackened stems

RECOGNISE

Leaves yellow and shrivel as roots and stem bases turn brown or black and decay.

ACT

Lift badly affected plants. Rotten roots cannot be restored; improve drainage before replanting.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and avoid conditions that leave roots persistently wet. Investigate recurring losses before replanting.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 107

Beetroot
Troubles

Protect young seedlings and keep roots growing steadily. Check leaf damage, bolting and root quality separately. Confirm nutrient problems before adding trace elements, and lift sound roots before prolonged autumn wet or severe frost.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEETROOT

Blackleg
RECOGNISE

Seedlings blacken, shrivel and may collapse. Crowding, poor drainage and excess moisture favour seedling disease.

ACT

Remove collapsed seedlings. Correct excess wetness; affected plants will not recover.

PREVENT

Sow thinly in well-drained ground. For modules, use fresh seed compost and clean trays; avoid overwatering.

BEETROOT

Bolting
RECOGNISE

A flower stem forms before a useful root develops. Cold during early growth or hot, dry conditions can trigger bolting.

ACT

Remove bolted plants; sow replacements when conditions are suitable.

PREVENT

Use Boltardy for protected early sowings, or sow as spring warms. Maintain moisture and thin direct sowings promptly.

BEETROOT

Leaf Spot

Spotted leaves

RECOGNISE

Brown spots may develop pale centres that fall out. Light spotting may have little effect; severe leaf loss can check growth.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves; minor spotting seldom needs intervention.

PREVENT

Rotate crops and prepare adequately nourished soil before sowing.

BEETROOT

Fanging
RECOGNISE

Roots divide or fork, often where fresh manure, stones or poorly prepared heavy soil interrupt growth.

ACT

Existing forked roots will not straighten.

PREVENT

Use ground manured for a previous crop, or well-rotted compost added in autumn. Remove stones and prepare the soil well.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 108

Beetroot
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

BEETROOT

Beet Leaf Miner (Mangold Fly)

Blistered leaves

RECOGNISE

White grubs mine leaves, making pale blotches that turn brown. Early summer damage checks young plants; flies are active April–September.

ACT

Remove mined leaves, or crush grubs within mines. Check leaf undersides for clusters of white eggs.

PREVENT

Use insect-proof mesh on a rotated site: overwintering flies can emerge beneath covers on old ground.

BEETROOT

Heart Rot

Blackened roots

RECOGNISE

Summer wilting, sunken brown root tops and blackened internal flesh can indicate boron deficiency, especially on dry, light or over-limed soil.

ACT

Check soil pH and confirm the shortage. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; damaged roots will not recover.

PREVENT

Maintain moisture, add mature compost and avoid unnecessary lime. Excess boron damages plants: never dose by guesswork.

BEETROOT

Autumnal Fungal Root Rots
RECOGNISE

Dark, decaying areas can develop on roots left in wet autumn soil. Appearance alone does not identify the cause.

ACT

Lift promptly. Discard rotting roots and check stored roots regularly.

PREVENT

Lift before prolonged wet or severe frost. Avoid harvest damage and store only sound roots in a cool, frost-free place.

BEETROOT

Speckled Yellows

Rolled leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow areas between veins may become brown; leaf edges roll inward. Manganese deficiency is one possible cause.

ACT

Check pH and moisture and confirm the cause. Seek an organic-compatible correction if needed; other deficiencies can look similar.

PREVENT

Avoid over-liming; maintain good soil condition and steady growth.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 109

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Check roots as well as leaves when brassicas wilt or stop growing. Mesh, sound transplants and steady growth prevent many losses; disease and nutrient problems need different responses. Test soil before liming or adding trace elements. Cabbage, cauliflower, sprouts and kohl rabi also have distinct quality problems.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

KOHL RABI

Woody Kohl Rabi
RECOGNISE

The swollen stem becomes hard and fibrous after drought, crowding, slow growth or late harvest.

ACT

There is no cure once woody. Use only parts that remain tender.

PREVENT

Grow steadily in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Space correctly, water in dry spells and harvest young unless using a variety bred for large tender stems.

ALL LISTED CROPS

White Blister (White Rust)
RECOGNISE

Raised white blisters, mainly beneath leaves, may also affect stems or flowers and distort growth.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and reduce crowding.

PREVENT

Avoid repeating brassicas on the affected ground the following season.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Pigeons
RECOGNISE

Soft leaf tissue is stripped away, often leaving stalks and veins. Winter and early spring damage can be severe.

ACT

Cover vulnerable crops promptly; stripped leaves will not repair themselves.

PREVENT

Keep taut netting well clear of foliage and secure the edges. Check frequently for trapped wildlife.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Leaf Spot (Ring Spot)
RECOGNISE

Ringed leaf spots can yellow foliage and cause leaf fall; wet weather favours spread.

ACT

Remove badly affected leaves and improve airflow.

PREVENT

Rotate brassicas; avoid the affected site next season.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 110

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ALL LISTED CROPS

Clubroot (Finger and Toe)

Swollen roots

RECOGNISE

Swollen, distorted roots accompany stunting, purple leaves and wilting in sun. Plants may temporarily revive when cooler.

ACT

Remove affected roots; do not home-compost them. There is no cure. Moving brassicas for only a few seasons may be insufficient: soil can remain infected for up to 20 years.

PREVENT

Use clean transplants, improve drainage and consider resistant varieties. Test pH before liming; long rotations do not guarantee clearance.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Cabbage Caterpillars

Large holes in leaves

RECOGNISE

Large holes in foliage and caterpillars inside hearts indicate cabbage whites, cabbage moths or related species. Check during the warmer months.

ACT

Inspect regularly and hand-remove eggs and caterpillars. Remove badly infested leaves.

PREVENT

Fit fine mesh before butterflies lay eggs. Keep it clear of leaves and secure the edges.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Flea Beetle

Small holes in leaves

RECOGNISE

Tiny jumping beetles pepper young leaves with small round holes. Seedlings are most vulnerable in warm spring weather.

ACT

Water damaged seedlings in dry weather so they can outgrow injury.

PREVENT

Protect susceptible young plants with insect-proof mesh. Raise strong transplants where direct sowings repeatedly fail.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Slugs and Snails
RECOGNISE

Irregular feeding holes and seedling losses are worst in damp weather. Look among loose leaves and open sprouts for hidden slugs.

ACT

Inspect after dark or in damp conditions and hand-remove slugs around vulnerable plants.

PREVENT

Raise sturdy transplants. Remove old yellow leaves and damp debris nearby; retain wildlife habitat elsewhere for predators.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 111

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ALL LISTED CROPS

Mealy Aphid

Insects on leaves

RECOGNISE

Waxy grey aphid colonies gather under leaves and on tips, often from June. Leaves curl and yellow; heavy colonies can leave sooty mould.

ACT

Check new growth; squash small damaging colonies by hand while leaving natural predators to help.

PREVENT

Remove old brassica stalks after cropping and encourage aphid predators.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Cabbage Whitefly

Tiny white insects beneath leaves

RECOGNISE

Tiny white flies lift from leaf undersides when disturbed. Honeydew may support sooty mould; established plants often tolerate them.

ACT

Usually tolerate them on outer leaves: damage to edible parts is often slight. Leaf crops such as kale need closer inspection.

PREVENT

Encourage natural enemies. Glasshouse-whitefly biological controls are not suitable for cabbage whitefly.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Diamond-back Moth

Skin-covered holes

RECOGNISE

Small green caterpillars feed underneath leaves, leaving thin windows of upper skin. Disturbed larvae may drop on a silken thread.

ACT

Inspect undersides and remove caterpillars on small crops.

PREVENT

Check through summer, especially where previous attacks have occurred; use well-secured insect-proof mesh.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Swede Midge

Blind plants

RECOGNISE

Distorted stalks near the growing point and blind growth may indicate swede midge. Look for tiny pale larvae and confirm the cause.

ACT

Remove badly affected plants. Seek confirmation before attributing unexplained blind growth to this uncommon pest.

PREVENT

Check young plants regularly and confirm unexplained growing-point damage.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 112

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ALL LISTED CROPS

Downy Mildew
RECOGNISE

Yellow areas above leaves correspond to white down underneath. Crowded young plants in damp conditions can be badly checked.

ACT

Remove affected leaves and severely diseased plants.

PREVENT

Use clean seed compost, avoid crowding and prolonged wet leaves, and use a fresh seedbed after previous trouble.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Cabbage Root Fly

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Root-tunnelling maggots cause wilting, blue-tinged leaves and checked growth. Young plants may die; older plants may fail to form good heads.

ACT

Remove badly affected young plants. Older plants sometimes recover if earthed up and kept growing; there is little to do once grubs are inside.

PREVENT

Fit close collars at planting or use fine insect-proof mesh. Rotate crops and remove infected roots.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Black Rot
RECOGNISE

Yellow V-shaped patches spread inward from leaf edges; veins darken and growth is checked. Warm, wet weather favours spread.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased plants. There is no useful cure in the source.

PREVENT

Use healthy seed and transplants, clear infected debris, rotate and avoid handling wet plants.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Wire Stem

Shrunken stems

RECOGNISE

Seedling stem bases blacken and narrow. Plants die or survive with slow growth and brittle stems.

ACT

Badly affected seedlings are not worth planting out.

PREVENT

Avoid cold, wet seed compost and crowding. Use clean trays and fresh compost.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Gall Weevil

Swollen roots

RECOGNISE

Local swellings near ground level may cause only slight growth checks. This is usually less serious than club root.

ACT

Usually no treatment is worthwhile. Confirm the cause if roots are extensively distorted or plants wilt.

PREVENT

Monitor affected plants; severe damage needs a fresh diagnosis.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Chafer Grubs

Roots eaten

RECOGNISE

Wilting plants may have damaged roots and fat, curved grubs in the soil. Recently cultivated grassland is more exposed.

ACT

Identify the grubs before acting; similar soil larvae are not always harmful.

PREVENT

Remove confirmed damaging grubs found during cultivation. Use nematodes only if labelled for the identified pest and suitable soil conditions.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 113

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Recognise → Act → Prevent

ALL LISTED CROPS

Cutworm

Severed stems

RECOGNISE

Grey or brown caterpillars hide just below the surface and sever young stems at ground level, often in June and July.

ACT

Hoe around affected plants and collect caterpillars exposed near damaged stems.

PREVENT

Where repeated losses occur, consider an appropriate nematode product, following its temperature and moisture instructions.

CABBAGE

Heartless Cabbages
RECOGNISE

Drought, poor fertility, shade, crowding or root damage can prevent firm heads. Check establishment and variety.

ACT

Check moisture and feeding; use balanced nutrition rather than adding straight nitrogen.

PREVENT

Choose a suitable sunny site, prepare fertile firm ground and plant securely.

CABBAGE

Split Hearts
RECOGNISE

Hearts split when rapid growth follows a check, particularly rain after drought. Freezing and thawing can also damage winter heads.

ACT

Harvest mature split heads promptly; do not expect the split to heal.

PREVENT

Keep moisture steady and avoid leaving mature heads standing too long, especially before severe cold.

BRUSSELS SPROUTS

Blown Brussels Sprouts
RECOGNISE

Sprouts become open and leafy rather than tight buttons. Loose soil, drought, crowding and other growth checks contribute.

ACT

Pick small tender blown sprouts for prompt use; remove larger spoiled ones.

PREVENT

Firm plants well, give adequate space and water in dry weather. An F1 variety may produce firmer sprouts.

CAULIFLOWER

Button Cauliflowers
RECOGNISE

Very small heads form early and soon run to seed after checks to growth. Pests, poor soil, crowding, drought or nutrient shortages may contribute.

ACT

Established button heads will not become normal full-sized curds.

PREVENT

Use rich firm soil, proper spacing and hardened-off plants. Water consistently and prevent early pest damage. Investigate suspected deficiencies before treatment.

CAULIFLOWER

Whiptail

Narrow leaves

RECOGNISE

Thin, strap-like cauliflower leaves and very small or absent heads suggest molybdenum deficiency, often associated with acid soil.

ACT

Confirm the cause and test soil pH; seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if needed.

PREVENT

Test pH and correct excessive acidity before the next cauliflower crop.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 114

Brassica
Troubles

All listed crops: Broccoli · Brussels Sprouts · Cabbage · Cauliflower · Kale · Kohl Rabi

Recognise → Act → Prevent

CAULIFLOWER

Boron Deficiency

Brown curds

RECOGNISE

Cauliflower leaves distort; curds may be small, brown-spotted or bitter. These signs alone do not confirm boron shortage.

ACT

Confirm the deficiency and check pH and moisture. Seek an organic-compatible correction; damaged curds will not repair themselves.

PREVENT

Improve soil with compost and keep growth steady. Excess boron is toxic: never dose by guesswork.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Magnesium Deficiency

Mottling between veins

RECOGNISE

Older leaves develop yellowing between veins, sometimes followed by reddish or brown areas.

ACT

Confirm the problem and check watering, pH and feeding. Seek advice on a suitable organic-compatible magnesium amendment if needed.

PREVENT

Improve light soil with compost. Avoid excessive potassium feeding, which can reduce magnesium uptake.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Frost

Cold-damaged leaves

RECOGNISE

Severe cold damages exposed heads and leaves, especially where plants are loose. Winter cabbages and savoys tolerate some frost.

ACT

Allow healthy growing points to recover. Remove rotting leaves and gently re-firm lifted roots.

PREVENT

Plant securely and earth up where needed. Harvest sound mature heads before severe weather when appropriate.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Cabbage Stem Flea Beetle

Tunnelled stems

RECOGNISE

Wilting plants may have cream-coloured grubs inside stems. Attacks occur mainly from August to October.

ACT

Remove badly infested plants after checking inside stems to confirm the cause.

PREVENT

Rotate away from affected ground rather than repeating brassicas there next season.

ALL LISTED CROPS

Manganese Deficiency
RECOGNISE

Yellowing between veins with curled or scorched edges can resemble other nutrient problems; one leaf is not enough for a firm diagnosis.

ACT

Check soil conditions and confirm the cause. Seek advice on an organic-compatible correction if required.

PREVENT

Maintain good soil condition and avoid unnecessary liming.

GROWING GUIDES

texts:
Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles

Carrots and parsnips share several root pests and diseases. Carrots are especially vulnerable to carrot fly; parsnips also suffer from old seed and canker. Start with fresh seed, deep well-prepared soil and a clean seedbed. Avoid fresh manure; use resistant varieties where available.

Recognise → Act → Prevent

PARSNIP

Old Seed / Poor Germination
RECOGNISE

Old seed, cold or dry soil and deep sowing can all delay or prevent emergence. Check conditions before resowing.

ACT

Sow again with fresh seed if the season still allows.

PREVENT

Use fresh seed each year. Keep the drill moist until seedlings emerge; a few radish seeds can mark the row.

CARROT

Green Top
RECOGNISE

Sunlight turns exposed carrot crowns green. Unlike green potatoes, green carrots are not harmful, but look unsightly.

PREVENT

Earth up around exposed crowns during the growing season.

PARSNIP

Parsnip Rust Fungus
RECOGNISE

Rust-coloured crown damage may resemble staining or canker; the precise cause needs confirmation.

ACT

Lift and discard badly affected roots.

PREVENT

Improve drainage, avoid root injury and seek a diagnosis before choosing a long crop break.

CARROT

Clayburn
RECOGNISE

Carrot surface damage associated with clay; check for pests or rot. The cause is uncertain.

ACT

Inspect affected roots; seek identification for recurring damage. Discard active decay.

PREVENT

Prepare well-drained, workable soil; use a raised bed where necessary.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot Fly

Tunnelled roots

RECOGNISE

Leaves turn reddish, then yellow. Maggots tunnel in carrots or damage parsnip surfaces. Seedlings may die; roots may rot.

ACT

No cure. Minor surface damage on large parsnips may be trimmed away.

PREVENT

Cover completely with insect-proof mesh on rotated ground. Sow thinly. Carrots sown after mid-May or lifted before late August may avoid peak attacks.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Fanging

Forked roots

RECOGNISE

Roots fork when tips meet stones, compaction or injury. Fresh manure and uneven seedbeds can contribute.

ACT

There is no treatment for an already forked root.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil, remove larger stones and avoid compaction or fresh manure before sowing.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 116

Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

CARROT

Small Roots
RECOGNISE

Crowding, drought, poor soil or pest damage can keep roots small. First check variety and maturity.

ACT

Check spacing, water and root health. Thin carefully and correct confirmed poor fertility.

PREVENT

Prepare workable soil in advance; maintain suitable spacing and steady moisture.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Splitting

Split roots

RECOGNISE

Roots split after heavy rain or watering follows a dry spell. Leaving mature roots in wet autumn soil also increases the risk.

ACT

There is no cure. Use split roots immediately; they will not store.

PREVENT

Water regularly and deeply in drought. Mulch with compost to steady moisture. Where splitting recurs, lift maincrop carrots before prolonged wet weather.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Sclerotinia Rot

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Soft root or crown rot develops white cottony mould, sometimes with black resting bodies. Both growing crops and stored roots can be affected.

ACT

Remove infected plants and rotten stored roots promptly; keep them out of home compost.

PREVENT

Store sound roots and check regularly. Clear infected debris, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Carrot-Willow Aphid

Distorted leaves

RECOGNISE

Greenfly cause distorted, discoloured, stunted leaves, especially in warm, dry summers. They can also transmit motley dwarf virus.

ACT

Tolerate small colonies; squash damaging colonies and encourage natural predators.

PREVENT

Inspect young crops and maintain steady growth. Aphid management cannot guarantee protection from viruses.

CARROT

Black Rot

Blackened carrot roots

RECOGNISE

Large black patches develop on stored carrots, often with no obvious symptoms before harvest.

ACT

Remove and destroy diseased roots promptly.

PREVENT

Store only sound roots in a cool, ventilated place and inspect regularly. Do not grow carrots on the same land next year. Avoid reusing a problem storage site year after year.

CARROT

Carrot Motley Dwarf

Discoloured leaves

RECOGNISE

Yellow mottling, red outer leaves and stunting may indicate carrot motley dwarf, an aphid-transmitted virus complex.

ACT

Confirm the cause and remove badly affected plants; infected plants cannot be cured.

PREVENT

Inspect young growth, encourage aphid predators and remove damaging colonies. Virus spread can still occur.

GROWING GUIDES
IMPERIAL · 117

Carrot and Parsnip
Troubles
Recognise → Act → Prevent

PARSNIP

Parsnip Canker

Blackened parsnip roots

RECOGNISE

Brown or black rot and cracking around the crown. Damage can spread downwards in wet, heavy soil; large roots suffer most.

ACT

No cure. Trim damage and use sound roots promptly. Destroy badly rotten roots; do not store them.

PREVENT

Choose resistant varieties such as Gladiator, White Gem or Avonresister. Test pH before liming; avoid fresh manure or unfinished compost. Prepare well-drained soil. Where canker recurs, sow later for smaller roots.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Violet Root Rot

Mouldy roots

RECOGNISE

Foliage may yellow slightly. Lifted roots show a felt-like coating of purple fungal threads, especially on the lower parts.

ACT

There is no cure. Destroy diseased roots.

PREVENT

Keep affected roots out of storage. Remove infected roots, avoid moving soil and seek crop-break advice if losses recur.

CARROT / PARSNIP

Swift Moth

Hollowed-out roots

RECOGNISE

Soil-living caterpillars hollow out roots and may move backwards when disturbed. Affected plants can lose vigour.

ACT

Inspect soil beside damaged roots; hand-remove caterpillars. Discard badly damaged or rotting roots.

PREVENT

Check vulnerable plants. For recurring losses, consider suitable biological nematodes with supplier guidance.

GROWING GUIDES
